summary:
Çanakkale province stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward LGBT people has been formalised as state policy. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions, 256 of them recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record. Street-level identity checks remain a routine encounter for visitors: in 2025 Istanbul police stopped some 20 trans women in Beyoğlu and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for GBT background checks before release, and foreign nationals stopped at such checkpoints must produce original identity documents, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Any checkpoint interaction is therefore an occasion on which a passport can be compared against presentation.

A draft omnibus law known as the 11th Judicial Package was reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. The leaked text would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" and would criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony, with penalties of up to four years in prison. It would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care, including surgery, from 18 to 25 and require permanent infertility as a condition, and would punish health professionals who perform such care. Human Rights Watch describes it as one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades. The Erdoğan government has framed its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, titled "A major siege against LGBTI+ people in 2025: Hostility turned into state policy", was launched by lawyer Kerem Dikmen and finds that anti-LGBTI+ hostility has become institutionalised as explicit policy. Senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a "Year of the Family" banner created a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, while regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricted freedom of expression and artistic freedom. The report's findings are presented as documenting a coordinated administrative posture rather than isolated acts of prejudice.
tangentialFactors:
The draft package had not been passed when Human Rights Watch reported it, and the measure's pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though prohibitions were already in force; detainees in Istanbul in 2025 were told the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was applied to them. Drafted norms and applied enforcement thus run ahead of one another, a pattern rights monitors describe as policy by instruction.

Opposition to the draft is organised and domestic: 15 Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association are recorded as opposing it. Kaos GL's reporting situates 2025 within a longer arc, noting that violations of international human-rights law monitored at Istanbul Pride events have continued since 2015, and legal experts cited in the Istanbul checkpoint reporting argue that GBT checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The country's violence record is documented separately from the legislative text. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker, who was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest.
localsOnly:
The age floor of 25 for gender-affirming care, including surgery, and the mandatory permanent infertility condition would fall on residents seeking transition-related care inside Turkey, as would the penalties directed at health professionals who provide it. The Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued, a change that risks profiling trans patients in official records.

Residents face criminal exposure under the draft text for participating in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies, and for behaviour deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality. Instructions issued to public institutions under the "Year of the Family" banner and the restrictiveness of regulatory and supervisory bodies shape what resident activists and organisations can publish, exhibit or organise.

Prison conditions are governed by registered sex and by segregation rather than gender-matched placement: a transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, and a trans man had been held in a women's prison. The Prison Insider country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners.
outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the 11th Judicial Package after the 29 October 2025 Human Rights Watch release is unresolved in the sources provided; the inventory records the text as a leaked draft under opposition, not as enacted law, and no later legislative outcome is sourced here.

No Çanakkale-specific enforcement data — detentions, checks, facility placement or incidents — appears in this inventory. The province-level record therefore rests on national findings and on Istanbul, Ankara, Kayseri and Sincan examples, which are cited as illustrations of the national pattern rather than as evidence of what occurs in Çanakkale itself.

Whether the draft's provisions on age, infertility and provider penalties would override the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation or operate alongside it is not stated in the sources. The internal reasoning behind the "other" option restriction and its effect on existing medical-board applicants are likewise not sourced here.
